title: Kodak Once Had a Nuclear Machine in Its Basement
summary:
For about 30 years, the film company Eastman Kodak kept an unusual machine in a secure basement in Rochester, New York. It was a nuclear device about the size of a refrigerator.

Kodak turned it on in 1975. The machine made a steady stream of neutrons. Neutrons are tiny particles found in the centers of atoms.

Kodak used the neutrons to test chemicals and find out what was in them. It also used them to make special pictures, a bit like X-rays. These pictures could show light materials, like water, that X-rays have trouble showing.

It might sound like a nuclear reactor, but it was built so that it could not keep a chain reaction going by itself.

The device ran until 2006 behind thick walls, under government security rules. Kodak and officials said it was tightly controlled. When it was taken apart, its uranium plates were carefully moved to a government facility. When people learned about it in 2012, many were alarmed. But the real story is a clever piece of Cold War engineering.
why_it_matters: It shows how scientists can use powerful tools safely by following careful rules.
